text:
Throughout my life, few experiences have shaped my identity as profoundly as the hours I spent in my grandmother's kitchen. What began as a simple curiosity about the meals that appeared on our table each evening evolved into a journey of self-discovery that continues to influence who I am today.

My grandmother, a woman of remarkable patience and unwavering dedication, immigrated to this country with little more than a suitcase and a collection of handwritten recipes. She rarely spoke about the difficulties she faced during those early years, but her cooking told the story that her words would not. Every dish carried within it a history of resilience, adaptation, and love.

It is important to note that I was not initially an eager student. At twelve years old, I found the process tedious and the instructions frustratingly imprecise. She never measured anything. When I asked how much salt to add, she would simply say "enough." When I asked how long to cook the onions, she would answer "until they are ready." This ambiguity drove me to distraction, as I had been trained by school to seek definite answers to definite questions.

Over time, however, I came to realize that her method was not imprecision but rather a different kind of precision entirely. She was teaching me to observe, to taste, to adjust. She was teaching me that some forms of knowledge cannot be reduced to numbers on a page. This lesson has proven invaluable in ways I could not have anticipated.

In my chemistry classes, I discovered that the same principle applied. While the textbook provided exact quantities and predicted outcomes, the laboratory rarely cooperated. Reactions proceeded more slowly than expected. Measurements varied. Success required not merely following instructions but developing an intuition for the material itself. My grandmother had prepared me for this reality long before I entered a laboratory.

The kitchen also taught me about failure. My first attempt at her signature dish was, by any objective measure, a disaster. The rice was undercooked, the spices were unbalanced, and the entire preparation had taken three hours longer than it should have. I was devastated. She simply tasted it, nodded thoughtfully, and told me to try again the following week. There was no criticism and no false praise, only the expectation that I would continue.

This approach to failure has fundamentally shaped my academic and personal philosophy. When I struggled with advanced mathematics during my junior year, I did not abandon the subject. When my first attempt at organizing a community food drive collected fewer donations than anticipated, I analyzed what had gone wrong and tried a different strategy the following semester. The second attempt served over two hundred families.

Perhaps most significantly, cooking with my grandmother taught me about connection. Food, I have learned, is a language that transcends the barriers of vocabulary and accent. When I prepare her recipes for my friends, I am sharing something that cannot be adequately translated into English. I am offering them a piece of a history that is not entirely my own but that I have been entrusted to carry forward.

As I look toward my future studies, I intend to pursue a degree in chemical engineering. Some might see this as a departure from the traditions of my family, but I understand it as a continuation. Both disciplines require patience, observation, and a willingness to fail repeatedly in pursuit of something worthwhile. Both demand that we respect the materials we work with.

My grandmother's hands have grown less steady in recent years, and she cooks less often than she once did. But the knowledge she transmitted remains, not as a set of instructions but as a way of approaching the world. It has taught me that mastery is not achieved through memorization, that failure is simply information, and that the most meaningful lessons are often the ones that resist easy explanation. These are the principles I will carry with me, into university and far beyond.

text:
For most of my adolescence, the prospect of speaking in front of an audience filled me with a dread that bordered on paralysis. What I could not have known at the time was that confronting this fear would become one of the most transformative experiences of my high school career, teaching me lessons about courage, preparation, and self-perception that extend far beyond the podium.

My difficulties began in the seventh grade, during a routine book report presentation. Standing before twenty-eight classmates, I found myself unable to produce sound. The silence stretched for what felt like an eternity. My teacher eventually intervened, allowing me to return to my seat, but the humiliation of that moment lingered for years afterward. I developed an elaborate system of avoidance, selecting courses and activities specifically to minimize any possibility of public performance.

This avoidance served me adequately until my sophomore year, when I became involved with an organization dedicated to environmental advocacy. I was passionate about the work and eager to contribute, but I quickly discovered that advocacy without communication is largely ineffective. The issues I cared about required someone willing to articulate them. I realized that my fear was not merely a personal inconvenience; it was actively preventing me from pursuing the causes that mattered most to me.

I decided to address the problem systematically. I began by researching the psychology of performance anxiety, learning that the physical sensations I experienced were not signs of impending failure but rather my body's preparation for a demanding task. This reframing proved surprisingly helpful. I then started small, volunteering to read announcements during homeroom, an activity that required only thirty seconds of exposure but that gradually built my tolerance.

Progress was neither linear nor comfortable. There were setbacks, including a particularly difficult presentation during which I lost my place and had to restart twice. But I persisted, and by the end of my junior year I had spoken at three school assemblies and one town council meeting.

The town council appearance remains the most significant. Our organization was advocating for the preservation of a wetland area that developers had targeted for a commercial project. I had three minutes to make our case before a panel of officials who had already heard from well-funded opposition. My hands trembled throughout, and my voice was not entirely steady. But I delivered the argument I had prepared, citing specific data about flood mitigation and local biodiversity.

We did not win that vote. The development proceeded, though with additional environmental protections that our advocacy had helped to secure. What I gained, however, was not measured in the outcome. I had done the thing I believed myself incapable of doing, and the world had not ended.

This experience fundamentally altered my understanding of fear. I had previously conceived of courage as the absence of anxiety, a state I would eventually achieve through sufficient practice. I now understand that courage is something else entirely: it is the decision to act despite anxiety, made repeatedly, until the action becomes possible. The fear never fully disappeared. I simply became someone who spoke anyway.

The implications of this lesson have extended into every area of my life. When I considered applying for a competitive summer research program, my instinct was to assume I would not be selected. I applied regardless, and I was accepted. When I contemplated starting a debate club at my school, I anticipated indifference from my peers. I organized it anyway, and eleven students joined.

I intend to study environmental policy, a field that demands both technical understanding and the ability to persuade. I know that I will face rooms full of skeptical people, and I know that I will be nervous when I do. I also know, now, that this combination is entirely survivable. The student who could not speak in the seventh grade has become someone who speaks precisely because it is difficult, and that transformation has taught me more about my own capacity than any easy success ever could.

text:
The fluorescent lights of my family's restaurant have illuminated nearly every significant moment of my adolescence. While my classmates spent their weekends at movies and sporting events, I spent mine folding napkins, taking orders, and learning lessons about work, dignity, and community that no classroom could have provided.

My parents opened the restaurant when I was seven years old, investing their savings and considerable hope into a modest space in a strip mall. The early years were difficult in ways I only partially understood at the time. I remember my father returning home after midnight, and I remember conversations conducted in low voices that stopped when I entered the room. What I did not fully grasp was the precariousness of the entire enterprise.

I began working officially at fourteen, though I had been helping informally for years before that. My initial responsibilities were simple: refilling water glasses, clearing tables, restocking supplies. I approached these tasks with the resentment typical of a teenager who would rather be elsewhere. I found the work tedious and the hours excessive, and I did not hesitate to communicate this to my parents.

My perspective began to shift during my sophomore year, when a regular customer named Mr. Delacroix suffered a stroke. He had eaten dinner at our restaurant every Tuesday for six years, always ordering the same dish, always sitting at the same corner table. When he stopped appearing, my mother noticed immediately. She learned from a neighbor which hospital he had been taken to, prepared a container of soup, and drove there after closing.

He recovered, eventually, and returned to his Tuesday table. But the incident revealed something to me about what my parents had built. The restaurant was not merely a business that exchanged food for money. It was an institution within a community, a place where people were known and noticed and missed when absent. My parents had created this without articulating it as a goal, simply by paying attention.

This realization transformed my relationship with the work. I began to learn the regulars' names and preferences. I noticed which customers came alone and lingered, and I made a point of speaking with them. I discovered that a restaurant, properly understood, is a service in the deepest sense of that word.

The work also taught me about labor itself. Our kitchen staff worked longer hours than I did, for wages that did not reflect the difficulty of the job. I watched them arrive before dawn and leave after midnight, and I developed a respect for physical labor that I suspect many of my academically-oriented peers have not had occasion to acquire. I learned to speak enough Spanish to communicate with the kitchen, and those conversations expanded my understanding of my own community considerably.

There were harder lessons as well. During my junior year, a customer became verbally abusive toward my mother over a billing dispute. I watched her absorb his hostility with a composure I could not have managed, apologize for a mistake that was not hers, and resolve the situation without escalation. Afterward, in the back office, I saw her hands shaking. She returned to the floor two minutes later, smiling.

I understood then that dignity is not the same as being treated with dignity, and that my mother possessed a strength that had nothing to do with the deference she was obliged to display.

I plan to study business, though not for the reasons that phrase might suggest. I am interested in the question of how enterprises can be structured to treat the people within them well, and I suspect that question has no simple answer. What I know is that I have watched two people build something valuable through years of unglamorous effort, and that the restaurant's fluorescent lights have taught me more about persistence, community, and the meaning of work than I could have learned anywhere else. Whatever I build in my own life, I intend to build it the same way.

text:
The first bike I ever fixed was a rusted Schwinn that someone had left by the curb on Alderman Street with a piece of cardboard taped to the seat that said FREE. I was thirteen. I wheeled it home with a flat rear tire, which meant dragging it, which meant that by the time I got to our driveway I had a blister on my palm and a very clear sense that this had been a mistake.

It took me four months to get that bike working. Not four months of steady effort, either. Four months of picking it up, getting frustrated, putting it down, and coming back to it when I couldn't think of anything else to do. The chain was the worst part. I did not know that chains came in different widths. I did not know that a chain could be too long. I bought the wrong one twice.

But in April it rolled, and I rode it around the block eleven times, and I have not really stopped since.

Our garage is now a bicycle graveyard that my mother tolerates with a patience I do not deserve. There are seven frames hanging from the rafters. There is a coffee can of bottom bracket cups sorted by nothing at all. There is a wheel I trued so badly that I keep it as a reminder.

What I like about bikes is that they are honest. If something is wrong, the bike tells you. A clicking sound means something specific. A wobble means something specific. There is no arguing with a bicycle and no way to talk your way out of a problem you have not actually solved. I find this restful. Most things in my life are not like this.

Two years ago I started fixing bikes for other people. This was not a plan. A neighbor saw me working in the driveway and asked if I could look at her son's brakes, and then she told someone else, and now there is a rotating cast of people who show up on Saturdays with bicycles and expectations. I do not charge, mostly because I would not know what to charge, and partly because the arrangement I have now suits me.

The person I have learned the most from is a man named Errol who works at the hardware store on Route 9 and who used to race, decades ago, in a category he refuses to specify. Errol does not teach so much as he stands nearby and makes noises. A particular exhale means I am about to strip a bolt. A different one means I have chosen the wrong tool. He has never once told me the answer, which infuriated me for about a year and which I now understand was the entire point.

Last spring I rebuilt a bike for a girl named Priya who lives four streets over and who had outgrown hers. I wanted to do a good job. I spent three weeks on it, replacing the cables, repacking the hubs, and finding a saddle at a swap meet that matched the frame color almost exactly. When she rode it down the driveway, she did not say anything, which I initially took badly. Then she came back around and did it again, faster.

I do not know yet what I want to study. People ask, and I say engineering, because it is the answer that makes the conversation end. The truthful answer is that I want to keep doing the thing I do in the garage, which is take something that does not work, understand why, and change it until it does. I suspect that description covers a lot of possible careers.

What I do know is that I have a coffee can full of parts, a blister that healed into a callus, and a fairly specific understanding of what it feels like to spend four months on a problem and then, one Tuesday in April, solve it.

text:
My brother Theo lines his cars up by color, not by size, and if you move one he will not shout at you. He will just put it back. Then he will look at you until you understand that you should not have done that. He is nine. I have been getting this look since I was eight and he was born, and I have gotten very good at reading it.

People ask me what it is like to have a brother with autism, and I never know how to answer, because I do not have a comparison. This is the only brother I have ever had. It is like asking someone what it is like to have brown eyes.

What I can tell you is specific things. I can tell you that the fire alarm at our elementary school was a particular frequency that made him fold in half. I can tell you that he learned to read at four by memorizing the closing credits of a nature documentary about tide pools, and that for a year he called all birds "cormorant." I can tell you that when he was six he did not speak for eleven weeks, and that when he started again the first thing he said was a complete sentence about the vacuum cleaner.

I can also tell you the harder things. I have missed things. I did not go on the eighth grade trip to Washington because the week it happened was a week Theo could not be left with a sitter. I have sat in hallways outside rooms where decisions about my family were being made by people with clipboards. I have watched my mother argue with an insurance company for ninety minutes and then hang up and make dinner like nothing happened.

For a long time I was angry about this in a way I could not admit to anyone, because being angry felt like being a bad person. What changed was a conversation with a woman named Ruth who runs a sibling support group two towns over. I went to one meeting expecting it to be useless. Ruth asked the room what we had given up. Nobody spoke. Then a girl named Marisol said "orchestra," and it broke something open, and by the end six of us had said things out loud that we had never said.

Ruth told us that resenting the situation was not the same as resenting the person. I had been unable to separate those two things for six years. It took one sentence from a stranger.

I still go, twice a month. I am now the one who sits with the new kids, which is a strange thing to be at seventeen.

Theo and I have a routine on Sunday mornings. We drive to the reservoir and we do not talk. He counts the herons. Last year there were as many as nine at once, which he considers a personal record though he did not cause it. I bring coffee and he brings a notebook where he writes the number and the date and nothing else. It is the least complicated hour of my week.

I want to study occupational therapy. This is not because of Theo, exactly, or not only. It is because I have watched a small number of very good practitioners do work that changed the shape of my family's life, and I have watched a larger number of mediocre ones waste our time. I know the difference from the inside, from the hallway, from the passenger seat. That seems like a useful thing to know.

Theo does not care that I am applying to college. He asked whether the campus has water. I told him there is a river. He wrote it in the notebook.

text:
I got a 34. Out of 100. The national qualifying threshold that year was 61.

My chemistry teacher, Mr. Okonkwo, found me in the stairwell between the second and third floors, which is where people at Roosevelt go when they do not want to be found. He did not say anything encouraging. He sat down on the step above me, which put his knees roughly at my ear, and said: "Show me question fourteen."

Question fourteen was a buffer problem. I had set it up correctly. I had used the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation correctly. Then I had taken the log of a ratio and inverted it, and everything after that was wrong in a way that looked confident.

"You know this," he said.

"Apparently not."

"No. You know this. You did not check it."

I had studied for eleven weeks. I had a binder. I had color-coded the binder. What I had not done, not once in eleven weeks, was work a problem and then go back and verify the answer against the original conditions. I had been solving forward and never backward. Every practice problem I got wrong, I had looked at the solution, said "oh, right," and moved on. That phrase — oh, right — turns out to be the sound of learning nothing.

The rest of that spring I did something tedious. Every problem, I solved twice. Once forward. Once by taking my own answer and running it back to see if it produced the given conditions. It roughly doubled my homework time. My grades did not improve immediately. For about six weeks nothing happened at all, which was demoralizing in a way that failure itself had not been, because at least failure is an event.

Then in October I sat the qualifier again and got a 78.

That is the part of the story that sounds like it should be the point. It is not the point.

The point is what happened in March, when I was helping a sophomore named Dagny with stoichiometry, and she got an answer, and I asked her to check it, and she said she already knew it was right. I recognized the tone. It was mine. I made her check it. It was wrong by a factor of two.

She was annoyed with me for a week. Then she was not.

I run a study session now, Thursdays, in room 214, usually four to nine people depending on what is due. The rule is that you do not get to say you understand something. You have to show that the answer survives being pushed back through the problem. People find this irritating. Dagny now enforces it more strictly than I do.

I want to study chemical engineering, and I am aware that this is a slightly absurd thing to want given that my defining experience of chemistry is scoring a 34. But I think that is backwards. Before the 34 I was good at chemistry in the way you are good at a video game — pattern recognition, fast, brittle. I did not know the difference between recognizing a problem and understanding one. A 34 is a very efficient way to find that out.

Mr. Okonkwo retired in June. At the thing they had for him in the gym, he found me and said one sentence, which was: "Fourteen." Then he went to talk to somebody else.

I have thought about that a lot. He taught for thirty-one years. He remembered the question.

text:
WRHS broadcasts at 88.1 FM to an audience that we have never successfully measured and that I suspect consists largely of the custodial staff and one man named Gus who calls the request line about twice a month.

The station lives in a converted supply closet off the band room. There is a hole in the acoustic foam shaped like Ohio. The board is a Mackie from 2004 that loses channel six if you look at it wrong, and the emergency alert system, which we are legally required to run, makes a noise at 3 a.m. that once caused a substitute night custodian to call the police.

I took it over in tenth grade because nobody else wanted it.

That is a less inspiring origin than the ones you usually read. But it turned out to matter, because a thing nobody wants is a thing you can actually change. Nobody had opinions about WRHS. There was no tradition to offend.

The first thing I found was that we had been broadcasting into a dead cable for somewhere between four and seven months. The transmitter was fine. The run between the closet and the roof antenna was not. We had been producing shows, on schedule, for most of a school year, into nothing. When I told the previous manager, he laughed. He had suspected.

I found the break with a borrowed cable tester and about six hours spread over three afternoons. It was above a ceiling tile in the corridor outside the auto shop, and it had been crushed by a bracket somebody installed for a projector.

After that I got interested in the question of who was actually listening, which is how I ended up doing something that I now think was the most useful part of this whole thing. I stopped assuming and started asking. We put a two-question survey in the lunch line for a week. Two hundred and forty people answered. The results were bleak and clarifying: eleven percent had ever heard the station, and of those, most had heard it involuntarily, in the cafeteria.

So we changed what we were. We stopped trying to be a music station competing with the phone in everyone's pocket, which was a competition we were losing by a margin best described as total. We started doing things that only we could do. We recorded the girls' soccer team's overtime win against Belmont. We did a twenty-minute interview with Mrs. Aldava about the forty-one years she has worked in the front office, which is now the single most-played file we have ever posted. We covered the school board meeting where they discussed cutting the bus routes, because nobody else did, and three hundred and six people listened to it, which is more than the number who voted in the student government election that year.

We are still small. The Mackie still loses channel six.

What I learned is not about radio. It is that "we have always done it this way" and "this works" are completely different claims, and that most institutions cannot tell them apart. WRHS had a schedule, a staff, a logo, and a broken cable. All of the visible parts of a functioning radio station were present. The only missing part was the part where sound left the building.

I want to study journalism, or maybe public policy — I have not settled it, and I am suspicious of seventeen-year-olds who have. What I know is that I want to keep doing the specific thing I did with the cable tester, which is refusing to accept that a system works because everyone says it does.

Gus called last Thursday. He wanted Creedence. We played Creedence.

text:
When my family arrived in this country, I possessed a vocabulary of approximately forty English words. Six years later, I am writing this essay. The journey between those two points has been the defining experience of my life, and it has taught me lessons about perseverance, identity, and the nature of communication that continue to shape my aspirations.

The initial months were characterized by a profound sense of isolation. I sat in classrooms where language flowed around me like water around a stone, present everywhere yet impossible to grasp. My teachers were kind but overwhelmed, and my classmates were curious but ultimately uninterested in the sustained effort that friendship across a language barrier requires. I ate lunch alone for the better part of a semester.

It is important to note that I was not a poor student in my native country. I had been considered academically capable, even advanced. The experience of suddenly being perceived as slow, of watching adults speak to me in the simplified register reserved for small children, was deeply disorienting. I began to understand that intelligence and its expression are not the same thing, and that the world frequently mistakes one for the other.

My progress accelerated through an unlikely source: the public library on Fremont Avenue. A librarian named Mrs. Castellanos noticed that I visited every afternoon and that I always selected books far below my reading interest but appropriate to my reading ability. She began setting aside materials for me, gradually increasing their difficulty. She never made an announcement of this arrangement, and we rarely spoke more than a few sentences at a time. But over two years she constructed a curriculum for me that no school had thought to provide.

This experience taught me that education often occurs outside of institutions, and that the most transformative teaching is frequently invisible. Mrs. Castellanos was not compensated for her efforts and received no recognition for them. She simply identified a need and addressed it with the resources available to her.

As my English improved, I encountered an unexpected difficulty. I found myself increasingly unable to express certain ideas in my first language, while simultaneously feeling that my English remained insufficient for genuine intimacy. I existed in a space between two languages, fully at home in neither. Conversations with my grandmother became halting. Conversations with my classmates remained slightly formal.

Over time, I have come to understand this condition not as a deficiency but as a particular kind of perspective. I notice things about English that native speakers do not notice, because I acquired the language consciously rather than absorbing it. I am attentive to the assumptions embedded in idioms, to the ways that grammar shapes thought, to the specific difficulty of translating concepts that exist in one culture and not another.

This attentiveness has directed my academic interests toward linguistics and cognitive science. I am fascinated by the question of how language structures perception, and I suspect that my own experience of moving between linguistic systems has given me an intuition about these questions that I could not have developed otherwise.

I have also become involved in supporting other students in situations similar to my own. For the past two years, I have volunteered with a program that pairs recently arrived students with peer mentors. I have worked with eleven students, and I have watched several of them progress through the same stages I experienced: the isolation, the frustration, the gradual emergence.

What I tell them, ultimately, is that the difficulty is temporary but the perspective it produces is permanent. They will eventually speak this language fluently. They will also always notice things that monolingual speakers miss. That combination, I have come to believe, is not a consolation prize for a hard experience. It is a genuine advantage, earned through effort, and it will serve them for the rest of their lives.

text:
The mosquitoes at Hobart Marsh are a specific problem that nobody warns you about properly. People say "bring bug spray." What they mean is that between roughly 6:40 and 8:15 in the morning, in late July, you will be inside a cloud, and the cloud will have opinions.

I spent two summers there. The first one was because my aunt knew someone at the county conservation district and I needed a job. The second one was because I wanted to go back.

The work is not interesting to describe. You walk transects. A transect is a straight line you have decided on in advance, and you walk it, and at fixed intervals you stop and put down a quadrat, which is a square made of PVC pipe, and you write down every plant species inside the square. Then you move. Then you do it again. My supervisor, a woman named Bett who has done this for nineteen years, can identify sedges from about four meters away, which I initially assumed was showing off and which I now understand is just what happens to a person after nineteen years.

I was bad at it for a long time. Sedges have edges, rushes are round — that is the rhyme, and it is true, and it is also almost useless in the field when the plant is half-submerged and has been chewed on. I misidentified Carex stricta as Carex lacustris so many times that Bett started making a noise when I said it.

The thing that changed was the data.

At the end of the first summer, I asked what happens to the sheets. Bett said they go into a database that goes back to 2004. I asked if I could see it. She said sure, in a tone that suggested nobody had asked before.

There were twenty years of quadrats. Same transects, same intervals, walked by a rotating cast of bored teenagers and one very patient adult. And when you plot it — I did this on my laptop over two weekends in September, badly, in a spreadsheet — you can see the cattails moving. Typha angustifolia. It comes in from the north edge where the culvert drains the road runoff, and between 2004 and now it has taken about sixty meters of the marsh, and it does not go backward.

Nobody had plotted it. The data existed. Everyone knew, in a general way, that there were more cattails. But the actual number — sixty meters, roughly three a year, accelerating after the 2011 road resurfacing — was sitting in a filing cabinet in a form nobody had looked at.

I showed Bett. She was quiet for a while and then she said "that's the salt," and then she explained about road salt and specific conductance and how cattails tolerate it and the sedges do not.

The second summer I still walked transects. But I also built a proper database, and I wrote a small script that flags any quadrat where the dominant species has changed from the previous year, and I made a map. The county used the map in a grant application. I do not know whether they got the grant.

What I took from this is not "I love wetlands," although I do. It is something narrower and more useful. Institutions collect enormous amounts of data and then do not look at it. This is not because anyone is lazy. It is because collecting is a job somebody is assigned and looking is a job nobody is assigned.

I want to study environmental science, with statistics. I am aware that this is an unglamorous combination. But somewhere there is a filing cabinet with twenty years of something in it, and I would like to be the person who opens it.

text:
I swam for eleven years and then I stopped, and the stopping is the part worth writing about.

Practice was 5:00 a.m. Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and 5:45 Tuesday and Thursday, plus afternoons, plus Saturday mornings at the Kettering pool because our pool was rented to the masters league. My best event was the 200 fly. My best time was 2:04.71, set in February of my sophomore year at a meet in Zanesville, and I never went faster than that again.

Not once. Two and a half more years. Never faster.

There is a specific kind of misery in getting worse at something you have organized your life around. It is not dramatic. Nobody notices for a while. You just post a 2:06, and then a 2:05.8, and then a 2:07, and the coach says something about taper, and you believe it, because the alternative is worse.

I did all the correct things. I changed my catch. I did dryland. I saw a sports psychologist named Dr. Weill for four months who was, I want to be clear, very good at her job. I kept a log. I ate the way I was told. In the winter of junior year I swam 2:04.9 at a dual meet and I cried in the parking lot because it was the closest I had been in twenty-two months and it was still slower.

Here is what I could not say out loud for about a year: I had stopped enjoying it somewhere around the tenth year and had not noticed, because enjoyment had not been a variable I was tracking.

I quit in March. I told Coach Petrosyan in his office, which smells permanently of chlorine and instant coffee, and he did not try to talk me out of it, which surprised me and then hurt and then, later, seemed like the kindest available response. He said "okay." He said "you'll want to tell the team yourself." Then he said one more thing, which was: "You were never going to be a college swimmer. You know that."

I did know that. I had known it for two years. But I had never let the sentence finish in my own head, and hearing someone else complete it was like having a splinter taken out.

The four months after were bad. I did not know what to do at 5:00 a.m. I did not know who I was to the eleven people I had seen every morning since I was six. I gained weight and then lost interest in whether I had.

What eventually filled it was not a replacement sport, which is what everyone suggested. It was a job at the Kettering pool, teaching six-year-olds. Level 2, which is the level where they learn to put their face in.

There is a girl named Odalys who was terrified. Genuinely terrified, not performing it. It took nine weeks to get her to blow bubbles. In week ten she went under, on purpose, for about a second, and came up furious and delighted, and I have thought about that second more than I have thought about any race I ever swam.

I do not have a lesson about persistence here. The honest version is that I persisted for two years past the point where persistence was useful, and the skill I actually had to learn was the other one: noticing that a thing has stopped working and being willing to say so.

I am applying to study kinesiology. Partly because I know a great deal about how a body moves through water. Mostly because I spent eleven years inside a system that measured one number and I want to understand the things it was not measuring.

My best time is still 2:04.71. It will always be 2:04.71. That is genuinely fine.

text:
Our robot was named Gerald, which was voted on, which was a mistake.

The competition was FIRST Tech Challenge, the 2024 season, and the task involved picking up plastic hexagons and placing them on a scoring rack. That is a sentence that makes it sound simple. It is not simple. A hexagon is a shape with no good grip surface and six equally plausible orientations, and a scoring rack in a gymnasium is at a height that changes depending on how level the gym floor is, which is never.

Gerald had a two-stage linear slide, a differential drivetrain, and a gripper that we redesigned four times.

Version one used two opposing servos and a rubber pad. It worked perfectly on the workbench and failed immediately at the first scrimmage in Dayton, because on the workbench the hexagon was always presented to us in the same orientation by a human being, namely me. On the field the hexagons are wherever they land.

Version two added a passive compliant wrist, which is a phrase I learned from a paper that a mentor named Sanjay sent us and that I did not fully understand for about three weeks. The idea is that instead of making the gripper strong enough to force the object into alignment, you make the joint loose enough that the object aligns itself as you close. It is counterintuitive. You are making the machine weaker on purpose.

It cut our cycle time by roughly forty percent and it cost eleven dollars in printed parts.

Version three was worse than version two. We built it anyway because our team captain, Reyna, had designed it and everyone including Reyna had gotten attached to it before we tested it. It took us two weeks to admit this. We lost a scrimmage. The specific failure was that the new gripper's wider jaw fouled on the rack uprights at exactly the height we scored most often, which is a thing we would have found in twenty minutes if we had tested it on a real rack instead of a cardboard mock-up.

Version four was version two with a slightly longer wrist.

I have thought about that sequence a lot. We spent eleven days building something worse because it was ours, and we spent two more days not saying so. Nobody was being stupid. Reyna is the best engineer on the team and she was the first one to eventually say it out loud. The failure was structural: we had no rule that forced a design to be tested against the previous version before we committed to it.

So we made one. It is written on the whiteboard in the shop and it says: NEW BEATS OLD ON THE REAL FIELD, OR OLD STAYS. It is not elegant. It has saved us at least three bad decisions since.

We went 6-4 at the regional and did not advance. Gerald is currently disassembled in four bins in my garage, except for the wrist, which is on my desk.

I want to study mechanical engineering. Everyone on my team wants to study mechanical engineering, and I imagine every FTC kid who writes one of these essays says the same thing, so I will try to say something narrower.

What I actually learned is that most engineering failures I have seen were not technical. Version three was not defeated by physics. It was defeated by eleven days of nobody wanting to tell Reyna, and by the absence of a rule that would have made telling her unnecessary. The compliant wrist was a genuinely clever piece of mechanical design and it took three weeks to understand. The whiteboard rule took ten seconds to write and it was harder.

Gerald was a bad name. We should have tested that too.
